items.title: Atoms in Motion
items.description: Start with the smallest things. A classic introduction to the atomic picture of matter, motion, and the practice of asking better questions.
items.note: Volume I · Chapter 1

cover.alt: Copper and teal particles moving along curved paths and meeting at an illuminated collision.

items.title: Seeing Theory
items.description: Make probability a little less abstract. Explore chance, distributions, and inference through interactive visual explanations.
items.note: Archived resource

cover.alt: A histogram of colored bars with a superimposed probability distribution curve.

items.title: Populating the page: how browsers work
items.description: Follow a page from its network request through parsing, layout, and painting. Look beneath a familiar everyday interaction.
items.note: Web platform

cover.alt: Three connected stages labeled HTTP, DOM and PAINT represent the browser rendering pipeline.

items.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
items.description: Get to know the tools behind the work: the shell, your development environment, version control, and debugging.
items.note: Tools for thinking and building

cover.alt: A terminal window displaying a Git status command and a ready-to-build message.

items.title: Work-Energy Theorem
items.description: Derive the work-energy relationship and use it to solve motion problems without calculating the complete trajectory.
items.note: Volume 1, section 7.3; text inspected

cover.alt: A plotted energy curve with a moving block and a direction arrow.

items.title: The elevator, the rocket, and gravity: the equivalence principle
items.publisher: Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute)
items.description: Use elevator and rocket thought experiments to understand free fall, weightlessness and the local limits of the equivalence principle.
items.note: Einstein Online 01 (2005); local-equivalence limits

cover.alt: A person in an elevator beside a stylized rocket, comparing gravitational and accelerated motion.

items.title: The Laws of Thermodynamics
items.description: Follow heat engines and reversible cycles to understand the first and second laws and the limits of converting heat into work.
items.note: Volume I, chapter 44; selected text sections

cover.alt: Pressure-volume axes with two distinct thermodynamic process curves.

items.title: Quantum Behavior
items.description: Compare bullets, waves and electrons to see why quantum probabilities require adding amplitudes before squaring.
items.note: Volume III, chapter 1; same content as I.37

cover.alt: Orbital wave paths and two narrow slits symbolize a quantum interference experiment.

items.title: The Doppler Effect
items.description: Explain changing pitch from moving sources and observers, then derive the corresponding sound-frequency shifts.
items.note: Volume 1, section 17.7; classical sound waves

cover.alt: Wavefront rings packed toward the direction of a moving source.

items.title: Applications of nonlinear systems
items.source: Notes on Diffy Qs: Differential Equations for Engineers
items.description: Use nonlinear differential equations to analyze a pendulum and a predator-prey system, with assumptions and limits made explicit.
items.note: Section 8.3; idealized pendulum and predator-prey models

cover.alt: A looped phase-space trajectory curves inward and outward around an equilibrium.

items.title: Induction
items.description: Learn to build a proof from a base case and an inductive step, starting with a concrete postage problem.
items.note: Third edition, section 2.5

cover.alt: A rising sequence of domino-shaped blocks evokes the steps of mathematical induction.

items.title: Generating Functions
items.source: Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, 3rd edition, §5.1
items.description: Encodes sequences as coefficients of power series, then builds generating functions using geometric series, substitutions and scaling. Worked examples emphasize missing zero coefficients and indexing. The section suits learners comfortable with sequences and algebraic series.
items.note: Third-edition textbook section; fourth edition exists but was not evaluated.

cover.alt: A distribution of coefficient bars beneath a formal power-series expression.

items.title: Probability Theory 101
items.description: Build probability from finite coin-toss spaces, then reason about events, random variables, conditioning and independence.
items.note: Author-hosted draft textbook chapter

cover.alt: A branching probability tree with conditional paths.

items.title: Planar Graphs
items.description: Distinguish graphs from their drawings and use Euler’s relation to understand why some graphs cannot be drawn without crossings.
items.note: Third edition, section 4.3

cover.alt: A connected planar graph drawn with nodes and noncrossing edges.

items.title: Building effective agents
items.description: Compare fixed LLM workflows with agents that choose actions from feedback, and learn when added orchestration is useful.
items.note: Published 2024; page warns tooling has changed

cover.alt: A model, tools and feedback nodes linked in a looping agent workflow.

items.title: Handling Overload
items.description: Understand why request rate alone can misstate capacity, and how services can degrade and limit work under overload.
items.note: Online book, chapter 21; sampled text

cover.alt: A service demand histogram rises above a dashed capacity limit.

items.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
items.source: Amazon Builders’ Library / AWS Builder Center
items.description: Choose timeouts and retry policies while accounting for side effects, overload, exponential backoff and synchronized retry bursts.
items.note: 2019 article; original library URL now redirects

cover.alt: Call, retry and success stages linked by arrows beneath a backoff timing annotation.

items.title: Microservices
items.description: Study the defining characteristics of microservice architecture and its links to team boundaries, ownership and operational tradeoffs.
items.note: James Lewis and Martin Fowler, March 2014

cover.alt: Several service nodes connect through a central event channel.

items.title: Asynchronous Programming
items.description: Build an understanding of callbacks, promises and async functions through code examples and asynchronous programming exercises.
items.note: Fourth edition (2024), chapter 11; code not run

cover.alt: Task, wait and resume stages linked along an asynchronous execution timeline.

items.title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
items.description: Learn how message events define a partial order and how logical clocks can produce a consistent total ordering.
items.note: Communications of the ACM, July 1978; PDF article

cover.alt: Multiple timelines with diagonal arrows showing the causal order of distributed events.

items.title: Natural Selection
items.publisher: UC Museum of Paleontology, University of California, Berkeley
items.description: Follow a hypothetical beetle population to understand how variation, inheritance and differential reproduction produce natural selection.
items.note: Evolution 101; reviewed/updated June 2020

cover.alt: An evolutionary branching diagram indicates variation and selection in a population.

items.title: Propagation of the Signal
items.description: Trace signaling from receptor activation through phosphorylation and second messengers to changes inside the cell.
items.note: Second edition, section 9.2

cover.alt: A circular cell with a nucleus and signaling arrows crossing its boundary.

items.title: Control of the Cell Cycle
items.description: Explains how cells pause or advance through G1, G2 and spindle checkpoints. Cyclins and Cdks provide positive regulation, while p53, p21 and Rb illustrate inhibitory control. Learners need basic cell-cycle knowledge; the account simplifies the wider signaling network.
items.note: Introductory textbook section, 2018; linked animation untested.

cover.alt: A circular cell surrounded by regulatory markers with G1, S and G2 checkpoints.

items.title: Operant Conditioning
items.description: Distinguish reinforcement and punishment, then compare how different schedules influence learned behavior.
items.note: Second edition, section 6.3; text inspected

cover.alt: Cue, action and reward stages in a behavioral reinforcement sequence.

items.title: Attention
items.description: Use listening experiments to compare models of selective attention and understand limits on processing multiple streams.
items.note: Noba authored module; sampled text

cover.alt: A bright circular attention field isolates some signals among many surrounding dots.

items.title: Strengthening the Student Toolbox
items.description: Translate research on retrieval and spaced practice into concrete study routines, while comparing them with less effective habits.
items.note: American Educator, Fall 2013; research-based guidance

cover.alt: Recall, spacing and repetition stages connected as a learning process.

items.title: Scientific Method
items.description: Examine how scientific methods are justified and why experimentation, statistical inference and pluralism complicate a single-method account.
items.note: SEP entry; substantive revision August 2026

cover.alt: Question, test and revise stages form a loop for scientific inquiry.

items.title: Epistemology
items.description: Compare accounts of knowledge and justification, including internalism, reliabilism and foundational structures.
items.note: SEP entry; selected knowledge/justification sections

cover.alt: Layered blocks of justification form a conceptual foundation.

items.title: Pragmatism
items.description: Explore pragmatist approaches to inquiry, practical consequences and fallibilism, including disagreements within the tradition.
items.note: Authored encyclopedia article; update date unestablished

cover.alt: Idea, action and effect are connected as a practical inquiry sequence.

items.title: Formal Organizations
items.description: Compares voluntary, coercive and utilitarian organizations, then explains Weber’s ideal bureaucracy and Ritzer’s McDonaldization. Workplace examples invite learners to weigh efficiency, hierarchy and impersonality. Some employment and admissions details are historical generalizations.
items.note: 2021 textbook chapter; theoretical models, not current employment advice.

cover.alt: A branching organizational hierarchy with one root and multiple subordinate groups.

items.title: Collective Behavior
items.description: Distinguish forms of collective behavior and compare theories of how crowds develop norms, organize and act.
items.note: Third edition, section 21.1; theory comparison

cover.alt: An interconnected social network with additional crowd markers.

items.title: Social Institutions
items.description: Analyze institutions through roles, rules, power and interdependence, while separating social description from normative questions.
items.note: SEP entry; substantive revision October 2025

cover.alt: Four pillars support a lintel, representing durable social institutions.

items.title: Statistical Physics I
items.description: Develops probability distributions, thermodynamic ensembles and the statistical basis of entropy and temperature. Sampled notes connect microscopic states to bulk behavior, while problems ask learners to analyze impurities and gas fluctuations. Calculus is assumed.
items.note: Archived Spring 2013 course; sampled notes and problems, not every lesson.
items.observed_format: Course with PDF notes and problem sets

cover.alt: An ensemble distribution of colored bars with particles above it.

items.title: Coulomb's Law
items.description: Explains how charge, separation and direction determine electrostatic force, then combines forces from multiple charges using vectors. A hydrogen example distinguishes the classical model from quantum mechanics; learners need basic vector components.
items.note: Calculus-based textbook section, 2016; public text, restricted reuse.

cover.alt: Oppositely charged spheres joined by simplified field trajectories.

items.title: The Theory of Gravitation
items.source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, Chapter 7
items.description: Connects Kepler’s planetary patterns with Newton’s inverse-square law and explores what gravity explains. The chapter closes by explaining why relativity modifies Newtonian gravity. Its historical terminology needs care, especially when discussing light and mass.
items.note: Historical lecture chapter; modern relativity coverage is introductory.

cover.alt: A small orbiting body follows an elliptical path around a central mass.

items.title: Thermodynamic Processes
items.description: Distinguishes isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric changes using gas-piston examples. Learners compare heat, work and internal energy, understand why cycles return state variables to their starting values, and separate quasi-static from reversible processes.
items.note: Text chapter evaluated; linked process simulator was not tested.

cover.alt: Three different pressure-volume process curves show alternate thermodynamic paths.

items.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
items.description: Builds the equations of an ideal mass-and-spring oscillator from Hooke’s law. Worked examples connect period, phase, displacement, velocity and acceleration; a vertical spring shows how gravity shifts equilibrium. Basic trigonometry and derivatives are useful.
items.note: Ideal linear, undamped oscillator; chapter text and equations sampled.

cover.alt: A spring fixed to a wall stretches toward a block with a motion arrow.

items.title: Numerical methods: Euler’s method
items.source: Notes on Diffy Qs: Differential Equations for Engineers, §1.7
items.description: Introduces Euler’s step-by-step approximation of differential equations, comparing a numerical result with an exact solution. Step-halving exercises reveal error and instability, and a Runge–Kutta extension gives context. Prior derivatives and initial-value problems are assumed.
items.note: Section 1.7, version 6.11; examples inspected, code not executed.

cover.alt: Stair-stepped Euler approximations overlaid on a smooth differential-equation curve.

items.title: Binomial Coefficients
items.source: Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, 3rd edition, §1.2
items.description: Connects subsets, fixed-length bit strings and lattice paths as different ways to count the same objects. A rook-path investigation and solved subset problems help learners interpret binomial coefficients rather than memorize formulas. Basic sets are the prerequisite.
items.note: Third-edition textbook section; fourth edition exists but was not evaluated.

cover.alt: A triangular arrangement of nodes evokes Pascal’s triangle and binomial coefficients.

items.title: Trees
items.source: Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, 3rd edition, §4.2
items.description: Defines trees as connected graphs without cycles and develops the unique-path characterization through proof. Opening subgraph questions encourage discovery, while a family-tree example explains where everyday analogies fail. Familiarity with paths and elementary proof helps.
items.note: Third-edition textbook section; fourth edition exists but was not evaluated.

cover.alt: A root graph divides into branches and leaf nodes without cycles.

items.title: The chain rule
items.description: Teaches learners to identify inner and outer functions and differentiate compositions with the chain rule. Worked trigonometric examples and mixed-rule activities build toward nested expressions. Basic derivative rules are assumed; the formal limit proof is referenced.
items.note: Second edition, §2.5; text activities inspected, answer widgets untested.

cover.alt: Three linked stages show a function input transformed by composition.

items.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm
items.description: Explains Raft through replicated logs, leader election and safety rules. The sampled algorithm summary shows how terms, votes and log matching support consistent state machines under crash failures. This is advanced reading, with explicit majority and non-Byzantine assumptions.
items.note: Extended 2014 research article, 18-page PDF; selected sections inspected.
items.observed_format: Research article / extended technical report PDF

cover.alt: A leader node sends connections to replicas in a consensus cluster.

items.title: Service Level Objectives
items.description: Distinguishes service indicators, objectives and agreements, then shows how to select metrics that reflect user experience. Examples explain why averages hide bursts and latency tails. Learners can reason about targets, measurement windows and feedback for service reliability.
items.note: Book chapter; historical vendor SLA figures are not current guarantees.

cover.alt: A measured service curve crosses a dashed objective threshold.

items.title: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
items.description: Uses ambiguous network timeouts to explain why retries can create duplicate resources. Caller-supplied tokens, atomic recording, equivalent responses and retention limits form a safer API contract. Examples also cover delayed requests and reused tokens with changed parameters.
items.note: Engineering article; AWS example commands were read, not executed.

cover.alt: A request passes through an idempotency-key check to a single result.

items.title: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern
items.description: Explores how components receive their dependencies through a running movie-listing example. It compares dependency injection with service locators and weighs constructor, setter and interface styles. The lasting lesson is separating configuration from use; Java frameworks are historical.
items.note: Original 2004 essay; conceptual design reading, not current framework setup.
items.observed_format: Software architecture essay with Java examples

cover.alt: Client, interface and service modules illustrate dependency injection boundaries.

items.title: Using promises
items.description: Introduces promise consumption, chaining and error propagation in JavaScript. Contrasting missing-return and corrected examples show how floating promises cause races, then connect the same behavior to async/await. Learners should already understand functions and callbacks.
items.note: Guide text inspected; JavaScript examples and browser behavior not executed.

cover.alt: A chain of promise stages culminates in an error-handling branch.

items.title: References and Borrowing
items.description: Shows how Rust references let functions use data without taking ownership. Working and rejected examples explain immutable versus mutable borrowing, overlapping references and last-use scope. The chapter connects these rules to data-race prevention and assumes basic Rust ownership.
items.note: Official book section; displayed compiler errors inspected, not reproduced.

cover.alt: A borrowing reference points toward a labeled value inside a memory block.

items.title: Genetic drift
items.publisher: UC Museum of Paleontology, University of California, Berkeley
items.description: Explains evolutionary change caused by chance rather than selective advantage. Linked lessons use repeated marble sampling, bottlenecks and founder populations to show why small groups can lose variation. This is a conceptual introduction, without population-genetic derivations.
items.note: Main tutorial and two linked explanations counted as one learning resource.

cover.alt: A population-frequency histogram represents random changes in allele prevalence.

items.title: Transcriptome Fact Sheet
items.description: Defines the transcriptome and explains how RNA readouts reveal differences in gene activity between cells and tissues. Examples show how expression patterns suggest possible gene functions. It is a short conceptual guide, with older project descriptions rather than a sequencing tutorial.
items.note: NHGRI fact sheet updated August 17, 2020; link-only rights assessment.

cover.alt: Two strands linked by rungs symbolize RNA expression patterns.

items.title: Defining a species
items.publisher: UC Museum of Paleontology, University of California, Berkeley
items.description: Examines the biological species concept through interbreeding and reproductive boundaries. Spiders, look-alike birds and hybrids show why appearance alone is insufficient, while linked examples explain difficulties with asexual organisms, separated populations and fossil lineages.
items.note: Main page plus biological-concept extension; alternatives link timed out.

cover.alt: An evolutionary tree separates branches along a reproductive boundary.

items.title: Conditioning and Learning
items.description: Compares classical conditioning, which links cues with events, and operant conditioning, which links actions with consequences. Examples develop blocking and prediction error, then explain why extinction can suppress learning without erasing it. Suitable for introductory psychology.
items.note: Authored Noba module; citation year is not evidence of a 2026 revision.

cover.alt: Stimulus, association and response stages represent conditioned learning.

items.title: Judgment and Decision Making
items.description: Explores bounded rationality, overconfidence, anchoring and framing through decisions the reader can try. Equivalent gain-and-loss gambles reveal how presentation changes preference. The module offers a decision framework, while several calibration quiz facts are historical.
items.note: Introductory module; dated quiz facts are not current reference data.

cover.alt: Branching decision paths show how framing can change perceived choices.

items.title: Research Designs
items.description: Introduces experimental and correlational research, operational definitions and the roles of independent and dependent variables. Spending and happiness examples explain random assignment and confounds. Learners gain a framework for judging causal claims, without advanced statistics.
items.note: Noba teaching module; empirical examples illustrate design, not universal effects.

cover.alt: Random assignment separates test and control groups in a research design.

items.title: Models in Science
items.description: Surveys how scientific models represent, explain and support learning about target systems. Scale ships, gas models and fictional objects illustrate competing accounts and their limits. Readers examine why a useful model can simplify reality without being a literal copy.
items.note: Scholarly survey revised April 2, 2025; selected sections inspected.

cover.alt: Overlapping abstract frames compare a simplified scientific model and its target.

items.title: Scientific Realism
items.description: Examines what it means to believe scientific theories describe unobservable reality. It separates the aims and achievements of science, then analyzes underdetermination and realist replies. This advanced survey helps readers compare positions rather than settle the debate by authority.
items.note: Revised June 12, 2017; philosophical arguments are contested positions.

cover.alt: Nested orbital lines and an observation arrow evoke the question of reality behind scientific models.

items.title: Counterfactual Theories of Causation
items.description: Develops counterfactual accounts of causation and tests them against difficult cases. The Suzy-and-Billy bottle example shows why simple dependence can fail when one cause preempts another. Readers compare proposed repairs; the article assumes comfort with philosophical logic.
items.note: Revised April 1, 2024; sampled arguments, not a causal-estimation manual.

cover.alt: Alternative branches labeled IF and ELSE represent counterfactual possibilities.

items.title: Virtue Ethics
items.description: Explains virtue ethics through character, practical wisdom and reasons for action, contrasting its emphasis with duties and consequences. Honesty examples and the action-guidance objection show how the theory handles choices. The account presents normative arguments, not personality science.
items.note: Revised May 3, 2026; introductory and objection sections sampled.

cover.alt: A balanced scale represents ethical judgment and practical wisdom.

items.title: 1.1. What Is Sociology?
items.description: Introduces sociological analysis at micro, macro and global scales. Everyday coordination and Mills’s distinction between private troubles and public issues explain how agency relates to social structure. The section also warns against treating “society” as an independent actor.
items.note: 2023 Canadian adaptation; distinct introductory scope from organization types.

cover.alt: A connected set of individuals spans a larger social field, representing micro and macro perspectives.

items.title: The Origin of Species: Lizards in an Evolutionary Tree
items.description: An educational short film follows island lizards to explain adaptation, reproductive isolation and evidence for evolutionary relationships. Habitat comparisons and DNA evidence connect observed traits with the process of speciation.
items.note: HHMI film with transcript; no embedding permission established.

cover.alt: An evolutionary tree and curved lizard-like silhouette evoke island lizard speciation.

items.title: Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
items.description: An adapted edition of David Hume’s inquiry into knowledge, causation and the limits of inference from experience. Reading the arguments on relations of ideas and matters of fact helps learners distinguish observed regularities from logical necessity.
items.note: David Hume; modernized Bennett edition; restricted adaptation rights.

cover.alt: Two spheres linked by a question-marked causal arrow evoke Hume’s inquiry into induction.
